title: Transient central hypoxemia due to intermittent high-degree atrioventricular block in a heart-transplanted patient diagnosed during routine electroencephalography: a case report
case_prompt:
A Swiss man in his 50s was hospitalized after a fall at home caused by recurrent short-lived episodes of generalized weakness, which over 8 years had increased to three or four times weekly and led to pelvic-ring fractures. He denied loss of consciousness, memory gaps, post-event confusion, tongue biting, or incontinence; there were no chest pain, dyspnea, or palpitations. His medical history included an orthotopic heart transplantation in 1991 for idiopathic dilated cardiomyopathy, paroxysmal atrial fibrillation (not anticoagulated), chronic immunosuppression with cyclosporin and mycophenolate mofetil, chronic kidney disease on dialysis, and a right pneumonectomy in 2006 for pulmonary carcinoma.  
Laboratory studies showed creatinine 513 μmol/L, urea 8.6 mmol/L, and hemoglobin 86 g/L; electrolytes, thyroid function, and inflammatory markers were normal. Protein electrophoresis and immunofixation were unremarkable. Radiographs revealed nondisplaced fractures of the right ischiopubic and iliopubic rami and left sacral ala. The patient’s prior cardiac follow-up—including multiple coronary angiograms, 72-hour Holter monitoring, and echocardiography—had shown only a high burden of atrial fibrillation and a left ventricular ejection fraction of 50%. On admission, the ECG was normal, and extended Holter monitoring was pending. An orthostatic challenge could not be performed because of the fractures.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Intermittent high-degree atrioventricular block — “we identified a 10-second period with transient third-degree AV block on the electrocardiogram trace.”  
2. Paroxysmal atrial fibrillation–related low cardiac output — “Initially, we suspected low blood flow caused by decreased cardiac output due to the paroxysmal atrial fibrillation bradycardia.”  
3. Orthostatic hypotension — “we also considered an orthostatic cause, but a Schellong test could not be performed due to fractures.”  
4. Neuromuscular disease — “we completed the investigations with a neurologic evaluation including EEG, even though neurological differential diagnoses such as neuromuscular disease or epileptic seizures were not at the top of the list.”  
5. Epileptic seizures — “the clinical presentation was not typical for focal with secondary generalization or focal to bilateral tonic–clonic seizures (no post‐ictal phase, no loss of urine or stool, and no bitten tongue)… absence seizures … would be rather unlikely given the first manifestation at age > 50 years.”  
6. Vasovagal syncope — “It is possible that our patient did not suffer from typical vasovagal episodes because of a transplanted and hence vagally denervated heart.”  
7. Ischemic process affecting conduction — “An ischemic process was suspected but reasonably excluded by coronary angiogram, which showed no significant atherosclerosis or vascular lesion requiring revascularization.”  
8. Medication-induced AV block (amiodarone) — “This episode had been attributed to the ongoing and recently introduced amiodarone treatment.”  
9. Medication-induced AV block (negative dromotropic agents) — “The patient did not take any medication with a negative dromotropic effect nor any drugs associated with occurrences of complete heart blocks.”  
10. Myocarditis — “The presentation was not consistent with myocarditis.”  
11. Graft rejection — “We did not find any clinical argument for graft rejection.”
